title: What is Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) — changes are appended to a log and fsync'd BEFORE the data pages are updated, giving durability (replay the log on crash) and enabling point-in-time recovery and replication — and how does it shape a ledger database's backup strategy (a base backup + archived WAL segments lets you restore to any moment)?
shortTitle: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and how it shapes a ledger backup strategy

s1_definition.profdef: Write-Ahead Logging is a durability protocol where every change is first appended to a sequential log and flushed to disk (fsync) BEFORE the corresponding data pages are modified. Because the log records the intended change durably first, a crash can be recovered by replaying the log. The same stream of WAL records enables physical replication to replicas and point-in-time recovery when combined with a base backup and archived WAL segments.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, before a clerk changes any balance in the big ledger, he first writes the exact instruction — "debit SAV2001 by 50,000" — into a sequential diary and makes sure the ink is dry (fsync). Only then does he update the ledger page. If the power fails mid-update, the bank reopens the diary and re-applies every instruction that was written down, so no committed transaction is ever lost, and the ledger is reconstructed exactly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Log the change durably first, update the data pages after — so a crash is recovered by replaying the log, and archived logs plus a base backup let you restore to any moment.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Write-Ahead Logging is a durability protocol where every change is first appended to a sequential log and flushed to disk (fsync) BEFORE the corresponding data pages are modified. Because the log records the intended change durably first, a crash can be recovered by replaying the log. The same stream of WAL records enables physical replication to replicas and point-in-time recovery when combined with a base backup and archived WAL segments.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, before a clerk changes any balance in the big ledger, he first writes the exact instruction — "debit SAV2001 by 50,000" — into a sequential diary and makes sure the ink is dry (fsync). Only then does he update the ledger page. If the power fails mid-update, the bank reopens the diary and re-applies every instruction that was written down, so no committed transaction is ever lost, and the ledger is reconstructed exactly.

**One line to remember:** Log the change durably first, update the data pages after — so a crash is recovered by replaying the log, and archived logs plus a base backup let you restore to any moment.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem WAL solves is the gap between "the transaction said COMMIT" and "the data pages are safely on disk." Writing the actual data pages randomly across disk on every commit would be slow, and a crash in the middle would corrupt the database. WAL decouples durability from the physical page writes.

When a transaction commits, PostgreSQL appends compact records describing the change to the WAL — a sequential file — and calls fsync so those records are physically on disk before it reports success. Sequential appends are fast. The actual data pages in the buffer cache are flushed to their random locations later, in the background, by the checkpointer. This is the "write-ahead" guarantee: the log is ahead of the data.

Durability on crash: if the server dies, on restart it reads the WAL from the last checkpoint forward and replays every committed change against the data files, redoing anything that had not yet been flushed. Any transaction that had committed is recovered; any that had not is discarded. This is crash recovery, and it is why a committed transfer is never lost.

Replication: a replica is just another server replaying the same WAL stream. The primary ships WAL records to replicas, which apply them to stay in sync. Streaming replication sends WAL continuously; this is how read replicas and standbys work.

Point-in-time recovery (PITR): this is the heart of a ledger backup strategy. You take a base backup — a full physical copy of the data directory — at some moment, then continuously archive every WAL segment the database fills. To recover, you restore the base backup and replay archived WAL up to any chosen timestamp or transaction. That means you can restore to "9:59:59 AM, one second before the bad batch job ran," not just to last night's snapshot.

For a ledger database this is decisive. A ledger must be auditable and must never lose a committed entry. The backup strategy is therefore: a periodic base backup plus continuous WAL archiving to durable storage like S3. This gives a recovery point objective of essentially zero committed-data loss, because every committed transaction is in an archived WAL segment, and it gives surgical recovery to any moment, which is exactly what you need to undo a faulty migration or a corrupting job without losing the good transactions that followed earlier.

Operational notes: checkpoints bound how much WAL must be replayed on recovery; more frequent checkpoints mean faster recovery but more write amplification. WAL archiving must itself be durable and monitored, because a gap in archived segments breaks the recovery chain. You periodically test restores, because an untested backup is a hope, not a strategy.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a transfer commits and the system reports success, but the server loses power one second later before the data pages are flushed. This is exactly what WAL protects against — on restart, the committed transfer is replayed from the log and is not lost.

Problem 2 — A faulty end-of-day batch at 10:00 AM corrupts thousands of balances. Last night's snapshot would lose a whole day of real transactions. This is exactly where point-in-time recovery helps — restore the base backup and replay WAL up to 9:59:59 AM.

Problem 3 — The ledger must prove no committed entry was ever lost for audit. This is exactly why continuous WAL archiving matters — every committed transaction lives in an archived segment.

We will build a `LedgerService` whose transfers commit durably, and a conceptual `RecoveryRunbook` plus the archive and PITR configuration, showing base-backup-plus-WAL as the ledger's backup strategy.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__ledger.sql — an append-only ledger
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    direction   VARCHAR(6)  NOT NULL CHECK (direction IN ('DEBIT','CREDIT')),
    amount      DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    balance_after DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    committed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

INSERT INTO ledger_entries (account_id, direction, amount, balance_after)
VALUES ('SAV2001','CREDIT', 1000000.00, 1000000.00),
       ('CUR3001','CREDIT',  250000.00,  250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://ledger-primary:5432/ledgerdb
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        connection:
          provider_disables_autocommit: true
```

```ini
# ops/postgresql.conf.snippet — enable WAL archiving for PITR
wal_level = replica                     # emit enough WAL for replicas + PITR
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'aws s3 cp %p s3://nbi-ledger-wal/%f'   # archive each WAL segment
checkpoint_timeout = 5min               # bounds replay time on recovery
max_wal_size = 2GB
synchronous_commit = on                 # fsync WAL before COMMIT returns (durability)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/ledger-service-1.0.0.jar

# --- Ledger backup strategy: base backup + archived WAL = PITR ---

# 1. Take a base backup (full physical copy of the data directory)
pg_basebackup -h ledger-primary -D /backup/base -Fp -Xs -P

# 2. WAL segments are archived continuously by archive_command (to S3)

# 3. Point-in-time recovery to one second before the bad batch (ops/pitr-restore.sh)
#    restore the base backup, then set recovery target and replay archived WAL:
echo "restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://nbi-ledger-wal/%f %p'" >> /restore/postgresql.auto.conf
echo "recovery_target_time = '2026-10-25 09:59:59'"            >> /restore/postgresql.auto.conf
pg_ctl -D /restore start   # replays WAL up to 09:59:59, stops, promotes
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer of 50,000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, followed one second later by a power loss, and separately a corrupting batch at 10:00 AM.

Step 1: The transfer commits. PostgreSQL writes compact WAL records describing both ledger inserts to the sequential WAL file and calls fsync. Only after the log is physically on disk does COMMIT return success to the service.

Step 2: The actual data pages are still only in the buffer cache; the checkpointer will flush them to their random disk locations shortly. The log is ahead of the data — that is the write-ahead guarantee.

Step 3: Power fails one second later, before the pages are flushed. The data files on disk do not yet contain the new entries, but the WAL does.

Step 4: On restart, crash recovery reads the WAL from the last checkpoint and replays every committed change. The two ledger entries are redone against the data files. The committed transfer is fully recovered — nothing is lost.

Step 5: Separately, each filled WAL segment is archived to S3 by the archive command, continuously. A weekly base backup plus this unbroken WAL archive is the ledger's backup strategy.

Step 6: The 10:00 AM batch corrupts balances. We restore the latest base backup and set the recovery target to 09:59:59, replaying archived WAL only up to that instant. The database comes back exactly as it was one second before the bad batch, keeping every good transaction that happened earlier that morning.

```
2026-10-25 13:51:00 INFO  LedgerService - Ledger transfer committed (WAL-durable): 50000 SAV2001->CUR3001
[recovery] redo starts; replaying WAL ... recovery to 2026-10-25 09:59:59 complete; database consistent
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  COMMIT transfer 50000 SAV2001 → CUR3001
    │
    ▼
  1. Append WAL records → fsync to disk  ◄── durability happens HERE, first
    │  "debit SAV2001", "credit CUR3001"
    ▼
  2. COMMIT returns success to caller
    │
    ▼
  3. Checkpointer flushes data pages later (background)
         │
     ── CRASH before step 3 ──
         │
         ▼
     Restart → replay WAL from last checkpoint → entries redone → NOTHING lost ✓

  BACKUP STRATEGY (PITR):
    base backup (weekly) ──┐
    archived WAL segments ─┤──→ restore base + replay WAL to 09:59:59
    (continuous → S3)      ┘     → recover to ANY moment, undo bad 10:00 batch
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Write-Ahead Logging is the durability protocol at the heart of databases like PostgreSQL. The principle is in the name: before any data page is modified, the database first appends a compact record of the intended change to a sequential log and fsyncs that log to disk. Only after the log is physically durable does the commit return success. The actual data pages are written to their random disk locations later, in the background, by the checkpointer. Because the log is always ahead of the data, durability is decoupled from the slow, random page writes, and sequential log appends are fast.

This gives three capabilities. Durability on crash: if the server dies, on restart it replays the WAL from the last checkpoint and redoes every committed change against the data files, so a committed transaction is never lost. Replication: a replica is simply another server replaying the same WAL stream, which is how streaming read replicas and standbys stay in sync. And point-in-time recovery: by taking a base backup and continuously archiving every WAL segment, you can restore the base and replay the log up to any chosen timestamp.

That last capability shapes the entire backup strategy of a ledger database. A ledger must be auditable and must never lose a committed entry, so the strategy is a periodic base backup plus continuous WAL archiving to durable storage like S3. This gives essentially zero committed-data loss, because every committed transaction lives in an archived segment, and it gives surgical recovery to any moment rather than just last night's snapshot.

At the National Bank of India our ledger ran with synchronous commit so WAL was fsynced before any transfer was acknowledged, with WAL archived continuously to S3 and weekly base backups. When a faulty ten-o'clock batch corrupted balances, I did not lose the whole day: I restored the latest base backup and replayed archived WAL to one second before the batch, recovering to exactly 9:59:59 and keeping every good transaction from earlier that morning. The sentence I always remember is: log the change durably first and update the data pages after, so a crash is recovered by replaying the log, and a base backup plus archived WAL lets me restore to any moment.
